section.title: A Lament over Pharaoh
section.sectionRationale: The oracles against Egypt reach their end with a double lament: Pharaoh, pictured first as the primeval sea monster whose thrashing churns the waters, is netted and cast down under a darkened sky; then in a second dirge he is consigned to Sheol to lie among the very nations, Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, that already fill the pit with the slain.
section.thesis: Egypt's dragon-like pride, which churned the nations like the primeval chaos monster, is undone by the LORD's sword in Babylon's hand, and Pharaoh finds his only 'comfort' in discovering he is not alone among the uncircumcised dead.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the first lament, picturing Pharaoh as the monster of the seas brought down under a darkened sky; the sword of Babylon and Egypt's emptied land; and the second lament, consigning Egypt to Sheol among the whole roll call of fallen, once-terrifying nations.

units.label: The monster of the seas, and the sword of Babylon
units.note: the first lament, a darkened sky, and Egypt's desolation

verses.text: In the twelfth year, on the first day of the twelfth month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“Son of man, take up a {{qinah|lament}} for Pharaoh king of Egypt and say to him: 
‘You are like a lion among the nations; you are like a {{tanniyn|monster}} in the seas. You thrash about in your rivers, churning up the waters with your feet 
and muddying the streams.’

This is what the Lord GOD says: 
‘I will spread My net over you with a company of many peoples, 
and they will draw you up in My net.
I will abandon you on the land and hurl you into the open field. I will cause all the birds of the air to settle upon you, and all the beasts of the earth to eat their fill of you.
I will put your flesh on the mountains and fill the valleys with your remains.
I will drench the land with the flow of your blood, all the way to the mountains, the ravines will be filled.

When I extinguish you, I will cover the heavens 
and darken their stars. I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light.
All the shining lights in the heavens I will darken over you, and I will bring darkness upon your land,’ declares the Lord GOD.

‘I will trouble the hearts of many peoples, when I bring about your destruction among the nations, 
in countries you do not know.

I will cause many peoples to be appalled over you, and their kings will shudder in horror because of you when I brandish My sword before them. On the day of your downfall each of them will tremble 
every moment for his life.’

For this is what the Lord GOD says: 
‘The sword of the king of Babylon will come against you!

I will make your hordes fall by the swords of the mighty, 
the most ruthless of all nations. They will ravage the pride of Egypt and all her multitudes will be destroyed.
I will slaughter all her cattle beside the abundant waters. No human foot will muddy them again, and no cattle hooves will disturb them.
Then I will let her waters settle and will make her rivers flow like oil,’ declares the Lord GOD.
‘When I make the land of Egypt a desolation and empty it of all that filled it, when I strike down all who live there, then they will know that I am the LORD.’
This is the lament they will chant for her; the daughters of the nations will chant it. Over Egypt and all her multitudes they will chant it, declares the Lord GOD.”
In the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, wail for the multitudes of Egypt, and consign her and the daughters of the mighty nations to the depths of the earth with those who descend to the Pit:
Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be placed with the {{arel|uncircumcised}}!
They will fall among those slain by the sword. The sword is appointed! Let them drag her away along with all her multitudes.
Mighty chiefs will speak from the midst of Sheol about Egypt and her allies: ‘They have come down and lie with the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword.’

units.label: Among the fallen nations in Sheol
units.note: Assyria, Elam, Meshech, Tubal, Edom, and the terror-spreading nations, all already there

verses.text: Assyria is there with her whole company; her graves are all around her. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword.
Her graves are set in the depths of the Pit, and her company is all around her grave. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword, those who once spread terror in the land of the living.

Elam is there with all her multitudes around her grave. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword, those who went down uncircumcised to the earth below, who once spread their terror in the land of the living. They bear their disgrace with those who descend to the Pit.

Among the slain they prepare a resting place for Elam with all her hordes, with her graves all around her. All of them are uncircumcised, slain by the sword, although their terror was once spread in the land of the living. They bear their disgrace with those who descend to the Pit. 
They are placed among the slain.

Meshech and Tubal are there with all their multitudes, 
with their graves all around them. All of them are uncircumcised, slain by the sword, because they spread their terror in the land of the living.

They do not lie down with the fallen warriors of old, who went down to Sheol with their weapons of war, whose swords were placed under their heads, whose shields rested on their bones, although the terror of the mighty was once in the land of the living.

But you too will be shattered and lie down among the uncircumcised, 
with those slain by the sword.
Edom is there, and all her kings and princes, who despite their might are laid among those slain by the sword. They lie down with the uncircumcised, with those who descend to the Pit.

All the leaders of the north and all the Sidonians are there; they went down in disgrace with the slain, despite the terror of their might. They lie uncircumcised with those slain by the sword and bear their shame with those who descend to the Pit.
Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude, Pharaoh and all his army, slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD.

For I will spread My terror in the land of the living, so that Pharaoh and all his multitude will be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, 
with those slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD.”

qinah.gloss: A lament or dirge, the formal genre of funeral poetry sung over the dead. Ezekiel is told to sing this over Egypt while Pharaoh still lives, as if he were already dead.

tanniyn.gloss: A sea monster or dragon, elsewhere naming the primeval chaos-creature Rahab or Leviathan (Isaiah 51:9, Psalm 74:13-14). Casting Pharaoh as this creature makes his pride cosmic in scope, a rival to God's ordered world.

arel.gloss: Uncircumcised, a term of covenant disgrace in Israel's vocabulary. Applying it to Egypt and the other fallen nations groups their proud, terror-spreading might into one shared shame in death.

basic.context: This closes the oracles against Egypt with two funeral laments sung over Pharaoh while he is still alive. First he is pictured as a great monster of the seas, thrashing and muddying the waters, netted and hurled onto open ground under a darkened sky. Then, in a second dirge, Egypt is consigned to Sheol to lie among the whole roll call of once-feared nations, Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, already there.
basic.hermeneutics: These are real prophetic funeral songs, using the ancient qinah, lament, form and vivid mythic imagery (the chaos monster, the darkened heavens) to strip Egypt's pride down to size before it has even fallen. The point is not a literal zoological description but a declaration that no earthly power, however monstrous or terrifying, escapes God's sword.
basic.originalLanguages: Ezekiel is told to take up a qinah, a formal funeral lament, over a king who is still alive. Pharaoh is called a tanniyn, a sea monster or dragon, the same word Scripture uses elsewhere for the primeval chaos-creature Rahab or Leviathan, casting Egypt's pride as opposition to God's ordered world itself. And every fallen nation shares the disgrace of being arel, uncircumcised, in death.
basic.typology: The chaos-monster imagery used for Pharaoh echoes the same imagery Scripture later applies to the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, Revelation 12:9, 20:2. Just as God nets and slays the monster Pharaoh here, so Christ decisively defeats the ancient dragon at the cross, Colossians 2:15, and will finally cast him into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10.
basic.christ: The darkened sun, moon, and stars over Egypt's judgment, verses 7-8, echo the plague of darkness at the Exodus, Exodus 10:21-23, and anticipate the darkness over Calvary, Matthew 27:45, when God's judgment on sin fell on His own Son rather than on the nations who deserved it. And the chaos-dragon defeated here previews the ancient serpent's final undoing through Christ's cross and return, Revelation 12:9, 20:2, 10.
basic.god: God alone commands the depths, the stars, and the nations; He nets the great sea monster as easily as a fisherman his catch, showing that no power, however primeval or terrifying in its pride, escapes His sovereign judgment. Yet He is also the God who lets Pharaoh find his only 'comfort' in shared disgrace, a solemn, sobering justice rather than cruelty for its own sake.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 51:9-10 calls on the LORD's arm to awake as it did against Rahab and the dragon, the same chaos-monster imagery used of Egypt here. Exodus 10:21-23 records the plague of darkness over Egypt at the Exodus. Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 identify the ancient dragon as the devil and Satan, finally defeated. Colossians 2:15 shows Christ disarming every proud, monstrous power at the cross.
basic.oneStory: This is the last word against Egypt's pride: pictured as the primeval sea monster, Pharaoh is netted, his skies darkened, and his multitude consigned to Sheol among every other terror-spreading nation already there. It anticipates the far greater and final undoing of the ancient dragon himself, accomplished at the cross and consummated when he is cast forever into the lake of fire.

context.literary:
The chapter is two laments, and the second is a roll call. Verses 1 to 16 are a dirge in four panels: the accusation of the lion and monster in verse 2, the netting and scattering of the carcass in verses 3 to 6, the unmaking of the heavens in verses 7 to 10, and the sword of Babylon in verses 11 to 15, with a closing line in verse 16 that says who will sing this song. Verses 17 to 32 are a second oracle, dated two weeks later, that follows Pharaoh into the underworld and introduces him to its inhabitants.

The first lament works by pairing opposite images. In verse 2 Pharaoh thinks of himself as a lion on land and a monster in the water, an animal master of both domains. In verses 3 to 6 God reduces both to one: a creature dragged out of the water, flung onto the field and eaten by birds and beasts. The rivers that he churned and muddied are, in the end, settled and 'flow like oil,' verse 14, which is the strangest and quietest line in the chapter. Egypt's rivers stop being stirred.

The second lament is built on repetition. After the summons in verse 18, the nations are named one by one, Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north and the Sidonians, and each notice is sealed with formulas about being slain by the sword, lying with the uncircumcised and bearing disgrace. The repeated phrase 'in the land of the living' recalls the terror these nations once spread, and the same phrase brackets the end in verse 32. The effect is that of a graveyard tour: the guide names each plot and says the same words, and Pharaoh walks to the last empty grave.
context.historical:
The two oracles come from the twelfth year of exile. The first is dated the first day of the twelfth month, which is about March 585 BC, and the second is dated the fifteenth of the month in the Hebrew text, although a footnote shows the Septuagint reads the fifteenth day of the first month. Jerusalem had fallen the previous summer, and the news had come to the exiles in the tenth month, as Ezekiel 33:21 says. This is the first lament after the fall. It is notable that the prophet who had announced judgment on Jerusalem now turns to the nations that had once seemed to offer protection.

The ancient world expressed kingship through the images Ezekiel invokes. The lion was the royal animal throughout the region. The crocodile and the river monster were part of Egypt's world, and Pharaoh was the Nile's master in the royal ideology. The net is a hunting and war image that Ezekiel uses elsewhere of God's judgment on kings, as when He says He will spread His net over Zedekiah, Ezekiel 12:13 and 17:20. Here the net is God's, and the 'company of many peoples' is the assembled army.

The list of nations in verses 22 to 30 is a catalogue of powers that had already fallen or been humbled. Assyria had been destroyed a generation earlier. Elam, east of Mesopotamia, had been shattered by Assyria and is the subject of Jeremiah 49:34 to 39. Meshech and Tubal, Anatolian peoples of Genesis 10:2, were known as fierce and distant warriors. Edom and Sidon were Judah's neighbours. The lament works as a kind of necrology of the Near East.

The burial customs the oracle presumes are also part of the picture. Warriors were buried with swords under their heads and shields over their bones, as verse 27 describes. Egypt's own tradition was rich in elaborate burial, and being consigned to a shared pit among the uncircumcised was a deliberate insult to that tradition.
context.canonical:
The chaos monster is among the Bible's oldest metaphors for opposition to God. Psalm 74:13 to 14 praises God who smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea, Psalm 89:9 to 10 recalls that He crushed Rahab, and Job 26:12 to 13 says He shattered Rahab and pierced the fleeing serpent. Isaiah 27:1 looks forward to the day when He will slay the dragon of the sea. Isaiah 51:9 to 10 links all of this to the Exodus, and Isaiah 30:7 and Psalm 87:4 apply the name Rahab to Egypt. Ezekiel 32 stands in this tradition when it makes Pharaoh the monster that God nets.

The darkness over the nations belongs to the Day of the LORD vocabulary. Isaiah 13:10 says the stars and the sun will be darkened, Joel 2:31 says the sun will be turned to darkness, and the Exodus plague of darkness was a precedent, Exodus 10:21 to 23. The New Testament takes up the same sign at the cross, Luke 23:44 to 45, and for the end, Acts 2:20 and Revelation 6:12.

The picture of the dead in Sheol speaking to the newly arrived is found in Isaiah 14:9 to 11, where the kings rise from their thrones to greet a fallen tyrant. The phrase 'the death of the uncircumcised' was used of Tyre's prince in Ezekiel 28:10. It also draws on Jeremiah 9:25 to 26, which lists Egypt among the peoples uncircumcised in heart. The unusual closing of the chapter on a note of grim comfort reaches forward to Revelation 21:4, where death itself is ended and mourning is wiped away.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel meant his hearers to see that no empire is as large as its own terror. The lament teaches that the language of fear used for Egypt, a lion and a monster that churns the water, is the language God has already seen and conquered. He took the monster from the Exodus story and nets it again.

The long list of nations in the second oracle is meant to produce a particular feeling: that of coming to the end of a series. Every empire that had frightened the exiles has a plot already dug in the Pit. The terror these powers spread 'in the land of the living' is repeated until it becomes a refrain that rings hollow. The exiles are meant to stop being afraid of the empire that holds them, and to see that its own turn is not far away.

There is also a word for Egypt, and it is not wholly cruel. The lament is sung 'over' Pharaoh, a form of respect for the dead even when the dead are enemies, and the prophet is told to 'wail' for the multitudes of Egypt, verse 18. The God who sends the sword is also the one who bids His prophet weep. That tone is meant to protect the exiles from gloating.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what God will do and where the great powers end. It does not command anyone to dehumanise Egyptians, nor does it give a map of the afterlife to be treated as a complete doctrine. The picture of mighty chiefs who speak from the midst of Sheol, verse 21, is poetic and uses the ordinary ancient image of a shadowy underworld. It is not a lecture on the state of the dead, and it should not be used as a proof text for a detailed teaching about conscious existence after death. Other passages, Daniel 12:2 and Luke 16:22 to 23, give the fuller light.

What carries over is a sober awareness of the end of all human terror, and an invitation to weep over a fallen enemy rather than to enjoy it. The call to 'wail' for Egypt's multitudes models a way of speaking about judgment that does not celebrate it, which the prophet himself shows. A believer living under a threatening power can use the chapter to measure that power against the one who has already netted the dragon, and then pray for it.

debates.question: Does Ezekiel borrow pagan myth when he calls Pharaoh a sea monster?

views.label: A deliberate use of the ancient combat myth
views.case: Many scholars note that the Near East told of a hero god who defeats a sea monster to establish order. Rahab, Leviathan and the dragon appear in the Psalms and Isaiah in language that resembles this pattern, and Ezekiel's net and the monster on the open field belongs to it.

views.label: A polemical reuse that empties the myth
views.case: The Old Testament does not present a battle between rival deities. God does not struggle with the sea; He rules it, Psalm 89:9. The monster language is therefore used polemically, to strip away the claim of any power to be divine, and Ezekiel's point is that Pharaoh, not the monster, is a creature under God.

views.label: Rooted in Egypt's own world
views.case: A third view notes that the Nile crocodile was a familiar sight in Egypt's own world, and that Ezekiel is simply using the imagery of the region. The mythic echoes would still be there, but the immediate picture is local and natural.

debates.bearing: The three views agree that the image has an edge: Pharaoh is neither a god nor a primeval power, and the God of Israel has no rival. The Exodus is the nearest background, since there Pharaoh and his army were drawn into the sea, Exodus 14:27 to 28.

debates.question: What is the 'comfort' Pharaoh receives in verse 31?

views.label: Bitter solace in shared defeat
views.case: Pharaoh sees the other fallen nations and is comforted that he is not alone, a bleak consolation. This matches Isaiah 14:10, where the dead say to the fallen king, 'You too have become weak, as we are.'

views.label: Irony
views.case: The word 'comforted' is used with a bitter edge. It is the comfort a doomed man might feel looking at a long line of the doomed, and the text intends the reader to feel the poverty of such comfort.

views.label: A glimpse of real mercy
views.case: A smaller number of readers see a real alleviation, pointing to the fact that Egypt is in the end restored in Ezekiel 29:13 to 15. They note that Elam too is promised restoration in Jeremiah 49:39.

debates.bearing: The immediate sense is grim, and the passage does not hint at hope for the dead. The hope for the nations lies in the wider canon, such as Isaiah 19:22 to 25, and not in this closing scene.

study.originalLanguages:
The lament is a qinah, a funeral song, and verse 2 opens with a reversal of the usual practice: Pharaoh is addressed as 'a lion among the nations' and 'a monster in the seas,' but the genre tells the listener that the song is already a dirge. In verse 16 the song is said to be one that 'the daughters of the nations' will chant, so the lament becomes a public ritual. The mourners are the very nations Pharaoh once terrified.

The monster of verse 2 is the creature of Genesis 1:21, where God made the great sea creatures, the same word that appears in Psalm 74:13 for the dragons whose heads God smashed. The Septuagint commonly renders this Hebrew word by the Greek word for dragon, which links it to Revelation 12:9. The word is not itself a proper name; it is a category of dangerous sea beast, and in Ezekiel's use it carries both the Nile's crocodile and the primeval opponent of God.

The verbs of verse 2, 'thrash about,' 'churning up' and 'muddying,' describe a river creature that fouls the water. Verse 13 reverses it: 'No human foot will muddy them again, and no cattle hooves will disturb them,' and verse 14 has the rivers 'flow like oil.' The pairing of a muddied stream with a clear one is the point: the creature's restlessness was what fouled the water, and God's judgment brings stillness.

The darkness of verses 7 and 8 uses the verb of covering and the verb of making dark, language belonging to Exodus 10:21 and the Day of the LORD, Joel 2:31. The BSB's 'extinguish' in verse 7 is the language of a lamp being put out, which suggests a life or a dynasty going dark.

The word arel, 'uncircumcised,' appears in verses 19 to 32 and is the label of shame for the Pit. In the Old Testament it is mainly a ritual and cultural category for those outside Israel's covenant, though Jeremiah 9:25 to 26 widens it to the heart, so that even Israel can be uncircumcised. Egypt, whose people practised circumcision according to Jeremiah 9:25, is placed among the uncircumcised, so the word here marks the disgrace of an inglorious end, not a mere ethnic fact.

The terror these nations spread 'in the land of the living' is repeated in verses 23 to 27 and 32, and the motif of terror closes the chapter, when God says that He 'will spread My terror' there. What the great powers did to others, God does to them, in a deliberate echo.

typology.type: The monster netted and dragged ashore, Ezekiel 32:2 to 6
typology.fulfillment: The proud power is pictured as a dragon whom God drags out of the deep, a pattern that appears in Psalm 74:13 to 14, Isaiah 27:1 and Isaiah 51:9. The New Testament names the final dragon as 'that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan,' Revelation 12:9, and says Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities, triumphing over them by the cross,' Colossians 2:15. The correspondence is that a God who nets Pharaoh will net the greater enemy. The type is limited: Pharaoh is a human king under the figure of a monster, while the dragon of Revelation is a real spiritual adversary, to be thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10.

typology.type: Darkness over the land, Ezekiel 32:7 to 8
typology.fulfillment: The sun, moon and stars darkened over Egypt look back to the plague of palpable darkness, Exodus 10:21 to 23, and forward to the darkness over the whole land from the sixth hour to the ninth when Jesus died, Luke 23:44 to 45. Peter speaks of the same sign before the great Day of the Lord, Acts 2:20. The escalation is that in Ezekiel the darkness falls on a judged nation, while at the cross it falls over the one who bore the judgment. The type falls short in that Ezekiel's darkness is the sign of an enemy's end, while Calvary's is the sign of an enemy defeated by suffering.

typology.type: The descent into the Pit, Ezekiel 32:18 to 21
typology.fulfillment: Pharaoh is told to go down and be placed with the uncircumcised. Christ also goes down, 'to the lower parts of the earth,' Ephesians 4:9, and is in the heart of the earth for three days, Matthew 12:40, but He is not abandoned to Hades, Acts 2:27. The correspondence is the descent; the escalation is that He rises, and now holds the keys of Death and Hades, Revelation 1:18. The type falls short in that the descent of Pharaoh and the nations is the end of a story, while His is the middle of one.

typology.type: The lament sung by the nations, Ezekiel 32:16
typology.fulfillment: The daughters of the nations chant a dirge over Egypt, so that the judged power is mourned by those who feared it. In the end of the story, the kings of the earth and the merchants lament over fallen Babylon in Revelation 18:9 to 19, a deliberate echo of the funeral songs of Ezekiel and Isaiah. The contrast is that the lament of Revelation is followed by a rejoicing in heaven, and the type is completed in the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:1 to 9.

study.christ:
The chapter does not foretell a person, and its connections to Christ run through its two great images, the dragon and the darkness, and through its great enemy, death.

Start with the dragon. The Old Testament developed a language in which God's rule over the sea monsters stands for His victory over every force that opposes order. Ezekiel applies it to Pharaoh, and in doing so he places Pharaoh in a line that ends in the New Testament. 'The great dragon was hurled down, that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world,' Revelation 12:9. Colossians 2:15 says that at the cross Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross,' and Hebrews 2:14 says that through death He destroyed the one who holds the power of death. Ezekiel's net is a small picture of that larger victory. The one who nets Pharaoh in history nets the dragon at the cross, and the language Ezekiel uses of a public spectacle, a creature left out in the open field for all to see, is close to Paul's phrase about the powers.

Then the darkness. The sun, moon and stars are darkened over Pharaoh's death, verses 7 and 8, and the darkness is the sign that something cosmic is happening. Luke records that when Jesus was crucified, 'darkness came over all the land until the ninth hour,' Luke 23:44. In Ezekiel the darkness belongs to the judged. At Calvary it falls over the One who took the judgment on Himself. The same sign is used for the opposite reason, and the contrast is the gospel: those who deserved the darkness are given light because the Son went into it.

Then death. The long list of the dead nations, each with a company around its grave, is a grim picture of what death does to every kind of greatness. Paul calls death 'the last enemy,' 1 Corinthians 15:26, and thanks God for 'the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 15:57. Christ, who 'was dead, and behold, now alive forever,' holds the keys, Revelation 1:18. The whole parade of the dead in Ezekiel 32 stands for the thing He has beaten.

A caution is in order. Ezekiel does not equate Pharaoh with Satan, nor does he describe Christ's victory. The links belong to a shared biblical language of dragon, darkness and death, and the New Testament writers use that language when they speak of the cross.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is the one who has no rival in the depths. Pharaoh is a monster, and the monster is netted by a net that belongs to God, with 'a company of many peoples,' verse 3, as His hands. Nothing here requires a struggle: the verbs are calm and exact, spread, draw up, abandon, hurl, cause to settle. The God of Israel does not strain against chaos. He directs it.

He is the Lord of the heavens. 'I will cover the heavens and darken their stars,' verse 7. A king who thinks he commands the Nile finds that the lights of the sky answer to someone else. The darkness is not a natural eclipse but an act of the creator, so the oracle claims the sun and moon, which Egypt worshipped, as His servants.

He is the God of the nations and of their dead. The roll call of the Pit shows that He takes account of Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom and Sidon, none of them His covenant people. He knows where each lies and what each did. The Bible's God is not a tribal deity, and the oracle's last words, 'I will spread My terror in the land of the living,' show a justice that reaches all the way to the grave and back to the living.

He is also truthful about what judgment is like. The lament has nothing triumphant in its tone. The prophet is told to wail, and the nations sing a dirge. The God who punishes has not stopped being the one who says in 33:11 that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The same God who nets the monster also leaves the rivers 'flowing like oil,' calm at last, verse 14.

For worship, the chapter invites awe before a God who is not threatened by the most fearsome thing we can imagine, and a quiet humility that does not rejoice in the fall of anyone. It teaches us to sing a lament over the proud and to bless the God who holds the net.

crossReferences.note: Pharaoh is the monster among his rivers, hooked in the jaw, hauled out and left unburied on the open field. Ezekiel 32:2 to 6 returns to the same scene with the image of a net and a larger company, and the two oracles read as the first and last words on the monster.

God says He will spread His net over Zedekiah and he will be caught in His snare. The net of Ezekiel 32:3 is the same instrument turned on Pharaoh, which shows that the judgment on Judah's king and Egypt's is one act of God.

God smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea and fed the Leviathan to the creatures of the desert. The picture of a sea monster given to wild creatures to eat is close to Ezekiel 32:4, where the birds and beasts eat their fill of Pharaoh.

The arm of the LORD that cut Rahab to pieces and pierced the dragon is the same arm that dried up the sea at the Exodus. Ezekiel's treatment of Pharaoh as a dragon comes from this tradition of reading the Exodus as a victory over a sea monster.

The ninth plague was a palpable darkness over Egypt for three days, while the Israelites had light. It is the nearest precedent for Ezekiel 32:7 and 8, in which the heavens are darkened over the land of Egypt again.

Sheol stirs to greet the fallen king, and the rulers of the earth rise from their thrones to say, 'You too have become weak, as we are.' It is the nearest parallel to the scene of the dead speaking about Egypt in Ezekiel 32:21.

The prince of Tyre is told he will die the death of the uncircumcised at the hands of foreigners. The phrase prepares for the refrain of Ezekiel 32, and shows that Tyre and Egypt are judged by the same sentence of disgrace.

Jeremiah's word against Elam, one of the nations in Ezekiel's Pit, speaks of shattering its bow and scattering its people, and then of restoring it in the last days. It shows that the dead nations of Ezekiel 32 are not beyond the reach of God's later mercy.

Christ disarmed the powers and authorities, made a public spectacle of them, and triumphed over them by the cross. The pairing of a public spectacle with the dragon imagery of Ezekiel 32:4 shows how the New Testament reads the old victory over the monster.

The great dragon is hurled down and is identified as that ancient serpent, the devil and Satan. This is the New Testament's identification of the monster of the Old Testament poetry, of which Ezekiel's Pharaoh is one earthly shadow.

Darkness came over all the land from the sixth hour to the ninth, and the temple veil was torn. The cosmic darkness of Ezekiel 32:7 and 8, signalling judgment, is here experienced by the Son of God Himself.
The last enemy to be destroyed is death. After the whole roll call of Ezekiel 32, in which the proud lie in the Pit, Paul names the enemy that the chapter parades, and announces its end.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with God speaking order into the deep. Genesis 1:2 shows the waters and the darkness, and God's word sets bounds on them. The great sea creatures of Genesis 1:21 are made by Him, and the later poems take the language of the sea monster to describe whatever opposes His order. Ezekiel 32 is one of the places where that language is used of a human king, because the pattern of the fall is that people try to take the place of the maker, and the fruit of that is chaos, violence and terror 'in the land of the living.'

In the story of redemption, the sea monster is met at the Exodus. Pharaoh and his army are drawn into the sea and not one of them survives, Exodus 14:28, and Israel sings that God stretched out His right hand and the earth swallowed them up, Exodus 15:12. The prophets then remember the event as a dragon-slaying, Isaiah 51:9 to 10. Ezekiel 32 lets the memory speak again at the moment when Israel's hope of rescue by Egypt has failed and the remnants in exile need to know that the old God has not changed.

The passage sets up the larger conquest. The darkness of verses 7 and 8 gathers into the darkness at the cross, and the dragon is named in Revelation 12:9 and finally thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10. The Pit that holds the proud nations is entered and left by Christ, who now holds its keys, Revelation 1:18.

The story ends with a world where the monster and the Pit have no place. 'He will swallow up death forever,' Isaiah 25:8, and the sea is no more, so that there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The nations whose graves fill Ezekiel's list are not forgotten in that renewed world. Isaiah 11:11 counts Egypt, Pathros, Cush and Elam among the places from which God recovers His people, and Revelation 21:24 sees the kings of the earth bringing their glory into the city. The lament ends where the story ends, with every tear wiped away.

quiz.q: How does Ezekiel first picture Pharaoh in this lament, verse 2?

options.text: Like a lion among the nations and a monster in the seas, thrashing about and muddying the waters.
options.note: Verse 2 uses exactly this double image for Pharaoh's proud, destructive presence.

options.text: Like a fallen cedar tree, echoing the previous chapter's image.
options.note: The cedar image belongs to Ezekiel 31; this chapter's image is a lion and sea monster.

options.text: Like a shepherd who abandoned his flock.
options.note: Shepherd imagery for failed leaders belongs to Ezekiel 34, not this lament.

options.text: Like a watchman asleep at his post.
options.note: Watchman imagery belongs to Ezekiel 33, not this passage.

quiz.q: What happens to the heavens when God brings Pharaoh down, verses 7-8?

options.text: God darkens the sun, moon, and stars over Egypt.
options.note: Verses 7-8 state this darkening explicitly, echoing the Exodus plague of darkness.

options.text: A great earthquake shakes the land of Egypt.
options.note: No earthquake is mentioned here; the judgment is described through cosmic darkness.

options.text: Fire falls from heaven onto Egypt's cities.
options.note: The described judgment is darkness in the heavens, not fire falling.

options.text: Nothing unusual happens in the skies.
options.note: The opposite is true: the heavens are explicitly darkened over Egypt's downfall.

quiz.q: Whose sword does God name as the specific instrument of Egypt's judgment, verse 11?

options.text: The sword of the king of Babylon.
options.note: Verse 11 names Babylon's king directly as the coming instrument of judgment.

options.text: The sword of Assyria.
options.note: Assyria appears later as one of the already-fallen nations in Sheol, not as Egypt's coming judge here.

options.text: The sword of Edom.
options.note: Edom also appears later among the fallen nations, not as the instrument of judgment named in verse 11.

options.text: No specific nation is named as the instrument of judgment.
options.note: A specific nation, Babylon, is named directly in verse 11.

quiz.q: In the second lament, which nations does Ezekiel say are already lying in Sheol among the slain?

options.text: Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, and the princes of the north with the Sidonians.
options.note: Verses 22-30 name each of these nations in turn as already lying disgraced among the slain.

options.text: Only Assyria and Babylon.
options.note: The roll call names several more nations besides Assyria; Babylon is the instrument of judgment, not among the slain listed here.

options.text: Only the small nations bordering the Nile.
options.note: The nations named are major regional powers, not minor neighbors of Egypt.

options.text: No other nations are mentioned, only Egypt itself.
options.note: The entire point of verses 22-30 is that Egypt joins many other named nations already in Sheol.

quiz.q: What is Pharaoh's grim 'comfort' at the chapter's end, verse 31?

options.text: Seeing that he is not alone: all his multitude and army share the same fate as every other slain, terror-spreading nation.
options.note: Verse 31 states plainly that Pharaoh is 'comforted' only by this shared disgrace in death.

options.text: Learning that Egypt's throne will be restored after a short exile.
options.note: No such restoration is promised in this chapter; the tone throughout is unrelieved judgment.

options.text: Discovering that his descendants will avoid the same judgment.
options.note: The text speaks of Pharaoh and 'all his multitude' sharing the fate together, not an exemption for descendants.

options.text: Being spared from Sheol entirely because of his lament.
options.note: The opposite is true: verse 32 confirms Pharaoh himself will be laid to rest among the uncircumcised slain.

questions: Pharaoh is pictured as a great monster thrashing and muddying the waters around him, seemingly unaware of how exposed he is to God. Where might your own strength, busyness, or ambition be stirring up trouble you cannot quite see?

God darkens the sun, moon, and stars over Egypt's downfall, the same kind of judgment poured out at the Exodus and echoed again at the cross. How does knowing God has already judged sin fully at Calvary change how you face His discipline or correction now?

Pharaoh's only 'comfort' is finding he is not alone in the pit; there is no real comfort in shared disgrace. Where are you tempted to find comfort in the fact that others are struggling or failing just like you, rather than turning to Christ?

This chaos-monster imagery for Egypt's pride is ultimately defeated at the cross and finally at Christ's return, Revelation 20:10. How does the certainty of evil's final defeat give you courage for whatever 'monster' you are facing today?
The long roll call of fallen nations, Assyria, Elam, Edom, and more, shows that no empire's terror lasts forever. What are you trusting in today that this passage would call you to hold more loosely?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word translated 'monster' (tannin) elsewhere in Scripture names the primeval chaos-dragon, Rahab or Leviathan; some read it here simply as Egypt's well-known Nile crocodile, while others hear the fuller, cosmic overtone of a power opposed to God's ordered world.

The BSB's 'uncircumcised' renders a term of covenant disgrace; applying it to Egypt and these other nations groups them together in shame regardless of their earthly might, a deliberate irony given how feared each once was.

The reference to warriors buried 'with their weapons of war... under their heads' reflects an ancient burial custom honoring soldiers; the text notes these particular nations are denied even that dignity in death.
